title: A Disguised Traveller Finds Petra
text: Calling himself Sheikh Ibrahim ibn Abdallah, a pilgrim vowing to sacrifice at Aaron's tomb, the traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt followed a Bedouin guide through a narrow, dark gorge. Before him rose a building carved from solid rock. The Bedouin had long kept Petra's location a closely guarded secret, and his suspicious guide accused him of being an infidel hunting treasure.

source.name: National Geographic: Ancient Petra, Jordan's Lost Oasis

title: Iran's First Printing Press
text: As late as 1815 a British envoy wrote that printing was unknown in Persia. Then, around 1816-17, crown prince Abbas Mirza backed a press with movable type in Tabriz, run by the printer Mirza Zayn-al-Abedin. Among its first books was an account of a Persian-Russian battle, and a British doctor's guide to vaccination against smallpox probably appeared the same year.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Willem M. Floor): ČĀP (printing)

title: Peace Treaty on the Gulf Coast
text: By the late 1700s the Qasimi family of Ras al-Khaimah dominated the southern Gulf coast and grew rich from sea trade. After attacks on British and Indian ships, a British naval assault defeated them in 1819. In 1820 the main coastal sheikhs signed a general treaty of peace, the first of the agreements that turned their towns into the Trucial States.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: United Arab Emirates, History

title: The Night Aleppo Fell
text: At about 8 in the evening, a foreshock rattled northwestern Syria. Half an hour later the main earthquake struck, with an estimated moment magnitude of 7.3, wrecking Aleppo and damaging Antakya and Latakia. Researchers studying newly found historical records say at least 10,000 people were killed, and aftershocks kept shaking the region for months.

source.name: Geofísica Internacional (Darawcheh, Abdul-Wahed and Hasan): The Great 1822 Aleppo Earthquake

title: First Recorded Climb of Ararat
text: Local tradition said Noah's Ark still lay on Ararat's summit but that God had declared no one should see it, and Armenians honoured St. Jacob for trying and failing to reach the top. In September 1829 the German Johann Jacob von Parrot made the first recorded successful ascent of Great Ararat, at 5,165 metres the highest peak in today's Turkey.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mount Ararat

title: Copying the Cliff of Darius
text: High on a rock face beside the old road to Babylon, King Darius I had carved his victories in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Starting in 1835, Henry Rawlinson, an East India Company officer, became the first to reach and copy the inscriptions. His work cracked Old Persian cuneiform, and the other two versions were soon translated too.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bīsitūn

title: Tahereh Removes Her Veil
place: Badasht, near Shahrud, Semnan Province, Iran
text: In gardens near a small village east of Shahrud, followers of the Bab met to announce a break with Islamic law. Qorrat-al-Ayn, one of the Bab's earliest disciples, who received the title Tahereh here, argued for a radical break and won the debate. When she then appeared in public unveiled, many were shocked, and some left the movement.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Moojan Momen): BADAŠT

title: A Constitution for Ottoman Armenians
text: In the 1800s Armenians lived through a cultural renaissance, fed partly by contact with liberal ideas from Russia and western Europe. Inside the Ottoman Empire they shared in the Tanzimat reforms, and in 1863 the Ottoman government recognized a special Armenian constitution. Progress was slow, though, and Armenians in Anatolia still suffered many abuses.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ronald Grigor Suny et al.): Armenia, Modern Armenia

title: Georgia's Peasants Are Freed
text: After Russia freed its serfs in 1861, the peasants of Georgia, then part of the Russian Empire, began receiving their freedom too, from 1864 onward. Many found the terms burdensome. Old family-centred ways were already fading as schools and European ideas spread, and Russian, Armenian and Western entrepreneurs were opening mines, factories and plantations.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ronald Grigor Suny et al.): Georgia, National revival

title: Cholera Strikes the Pilgrimage
text: In 1865 cholera, probably brought by pilgrims from India, struck the holy cities of Islam with great violence, killing a third of the 90,000 believers gathered there. Returning pilgrims, travelling faster than ever by steamship, carried it to Mediterranean ports and onward to Europe, Russia and the Americas. In response, Europe and the Ottoman Empire built a vast quarantine system along the Red Sea.

source.name: EHNE, Sorbonne Université (Sylvia Chiffoleau): The Pilgrimage to Mecca, Epidemics, and Health Protection in Europe

title: Twelve Days Become Six Minutes
text: In 1868 Naser al-Din Shah let the Siemens brothers build a telegraph from Tehran to the Russian border at Jolfa. Its 480-mile double wire opened in 1869, and by January 1870 the line ran on through Tiflis, Odessa, Warsaw and Berlin to London. Messages between Europe and India that once took 12 days now took just over six minutes.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Michael Rubin): INDO-EUROPEAN TELEGRAPH COMPANY

title: Baku's Oil Goes Commercial
text: People around Baku had known about its oil since ancient times, and by the 15th century they were scooping lamp oil from shallow surface wells. Modern commercial drilling began in 1872. At the start of the 20th century the Baku oil field was the largest in the world, and derricks still stand in the gulf facing the city.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Baku

title: The First Shah to See Europe
text: Invited to the World Fair in Vienna, Naser al-Din Shah accepted and became the first shah ever to visit Europe. He left Tehran on 20 April 1873 and travelled through Russia, Germany, England, France, Switzerland and Italy. In Vienna, Emperor Franz Joseph received him with great courtesy, and the shah toured the fair and its Persian pavilion.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Helmut Slaby): AUSTRIA i. Relations with Persia

title: An Underground Ride up the Hill
text: Visiting Istanbul in 1867, Eugène-Henri Gavand saw some 40,000 people toiling up a steep, narrow street between Galata, the banking centre, and lively Beyoğlu. His answer was an underground railway, the world's second after London's. It opened on 17 January 1875 with a 2.5-minute ride, and carried 75,000 passengers in its first two weeks. Gavand skipped the opening ceremony.

source.name: Istanbul Technical University (Kayaoğlu, Kocabal et al.): Early Application of Underground Funicular 'Tunnel' in Istanbul

title: Painted Tombs of Sidon's Kings
text: In 1887 a royal burial ground at Sidon gave up a set of perfectly preserved Greek marble sarcophagi. Osman Hamdi Bey, painter and director of Istanbul's archaeological museum, secured them for his collection. The finest, nicknamed the Alexander Sarcophagus because people once thought it held Alexander the Great, still shows traces of its original paint.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Osman Hamdi Bey

title: Steam Train to Jerusalem
text: In 1892 a single-track railway opened between the port of Jaffa and Jerusalem, winding through the Hills of Judaea past spectacular views. For many years the line linked Jerusalem with the coast at Tel Aviv-Yafo and Haifa and with Beersheba inland, and before 1948 travellers could even continue by rail to Lebanon, Syria and Egypt.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Jerusalem, Economy

title: A Witty Reply Called Faults of Men
text: Annoyed by an older tract on how to discipline wives, Bibi Khanom Astarabadi wrote back in 1894 with The Faults of Men. Mixing Persian poetry, Qur'an verses, street songs and jokes, she spoke directly to her 'sisters' about husbands. It wasn't printed until 1992, but copies circulated, and one written in her own hand survives in Tehran's Majles Library.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Afsaneh Najmabadi): MAʿĀYEB AL-REJĀL

title: Thousands of Bricks from Babylon
place: Babylon, near Hillah, Babil Governorate, Iraq
text: In 1899 the German Oriental Society began digging at Babylon under Robert Koldewey. Locals had long reused the ancient baked bricks, so little of Nebuchadnezzar II's glazed Ishtar Gate still stood. But the team found thousands of small glazed-brick fragments in the rubble and collected them. Agreements in 1903 and 1926 let them take the pieces to Berlin, where the gate was rebuilt.

source.name: The Ancient Near East Today, ASOR (Helen Gries): The Ishtar Gate of Babylon, One Monument, Multiple Narratives

title: Hammurabi's Laws Found in Iran
text: Digging at Susa in southwest Iran in 1901-1902, a French mission led by Jacques de Morgan unearthed a basalt pillar 225 centimetres tall. It was covered in cuneiform laws in Old Babylonian, and on top a carving shows the sun god Shamash meeting King Hammurabi of Babylon, who reigned from 1792 to 1750 BCE. Today it stands in the Louvre.

source.name: Musée du Louvre, Collections: Code de Hammurabi, roi de Babylone

title: Shamakhi Shaken Again
text: Shamakhi, a former capital of Azerbaijan, had suffered many earthquakes, and in 1902 a huge one killed about 2,000 people and destroyed 4,000 homes. A researcher named Weber mapped its shaking using reports from 120 villages. More than 120 years later, geologists still found dropped keystones in a nearby chapel and argued the quake may have reached magnitude 7.4.

source.name: Tectonics, AGU (Pierce et al. 2024): Surface Rupturing Earthquakes of the Greater Caucasus Frontal Thrusts, Azerbaijan

title: A Line Drawn Across Yemen
place: Frontier between Ottoman North Yemen and British Aden, Yemen
text: In the late 1800s the Ottomans moved back into Sanaa and Taiz, while Britain had spread out from Aden to protect its hinterland. Clashes along the unmarked border grew, so in 1904 a joint commission surveyed it, and a treaty set the frontier between Ottoman North Yemen and the British south. Yemenis on both sides later saw it as outsiders meddling in their affairs.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Robert Burrowes et al.): Yemen, The age of imperialism

title: A Painter's Academy in a Palace
text: Court painter Kamal-ol-Molk had long dreamed of his own painting school. In 1911 the education minister Hakim-al-Molk set about helping him, and Iran's new parliament approved a budget and a plot in the grounds of the old Negarestan Palace. The Academy of Fine Arts became one of the achievements of the Constitutional movement, and he even lived there with his students.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Ahmad Ashraf): KAMĀL-AL-MOLK i. Life
